summaries.headline: English Teacher Uses AI Interrogation to Build Student Resistance
summaries.summary: A high school English teacher assigned students to interrogate Character.AI chatbots, expecting them to become addicted to the technology that never says no or pushes back. Months later, when offered another AI assignment, students responded with "Nah, that's old news," demonstrating they had developed cognitive resistance to the platform's appeal. The structured encounter suggests that controlled exposure to AI tools, paired with critical analysis rather than passive consumption, may help students build immunity to technology dependence.

summaries.headline: Home Visits Show Promise for Cutting Chronic Absenteeism
summaries.summary: Michigan schools that conducted frequent home visits to families of absent students achieved substantially better attendance outcomes than those using less intensive outreach, according to new research tracking student transitions across 2,700 schools between 2022 and 2025. Students in the most effective schools attended class about seven more days per year than similar peers in the lowest-performing schools — a meaningful difference given that missing 18 days triggers chronic absenteeism classification. The finding offers districts a concrete strategy for addressing attendance challenges, though researchers note that even the most improved schools often maintained chronic absenteeism rates above 40 percent.

summaries.headline: Anti-SEL Bills Stalled Despite Growing Legislative Opposition
summaries.summary: State legislators introduced multiple bills targeting social-emotional learning programs this year, with Arizona's GOP-controlled legislature passing a measure to repeal mental health instruction requirements before Democratic Governor Katie Hobbs vetoed it. Similar efforts emerged in Utah and other states, with critics arguing SEL serves as a vehicle for introducing divisive concepts into classrooms. The legislative battles signal ongoing political volatility around student wellness programming that districts have expanded since the pandemic, creating uncertainty for schools and vendors in the mental health education space.

summaries.headline: Detroit Pays 84% of High Schoolers for Attendance
summaries.summary: Detroit Public School Community District paid roughly 12,800 high school students — nearly 84% of enrollment — at least one $100 Visa gift card for perfect attendance during five-day cycles between January and March. The district's high school chronic absenteeism rate dropped 10 percentage points to 54% this year, down from 64% before the incentive program began. The broader reach suggests financial incentives can move attendance rates at scale in high-poverty districts, though the sustainability and cost-effectiveness of paying thousands of students hundreds of dollars each remains an open question for cash-strapped systems.

summaries.headline: Schools Embed SEL Skills Through Existing Technology Tools
summaries.summary: Districts are integrating social-emotional learning into regular curriculum using simple technology additions rather than standalone SEL programs. Fridley Public Schools in Minnesota has gained recognition for its approach, particularly with special education students, using tools like Think Nooks and existing software to teach emotional regulation and social skills. The shift reflects growing recognition that emotional intelligence skills complement academic learning and can be developed through everyday classroom technology rather than requiring separate platforms.

summaries.headline: NYC Gets Two-Year Extension on Class Size Mandate
summaries.summary: New York state lawmakers will give NYC until the 2029-30 school year to comply with class size limits, extending the original 2027-28 deadline by two years. The city now must bring 70% of classes into compliance this fall rather than the originally required 80%, with an additional 10% each subsequent year until full implementation. Mayor Zohran Mamdani's administration is banking on the delay to save hundreds of millions of dollars needed to close a multibillion-dollar budget gap, marking a shift from his campaign promise to swiftly implement the law he voted for as a state assemblyman.

summaries.headline: Vermont District Defies Federal Pressure on Immigration Policy
summaries.summary: Winooski School District in Vermont has maintained its sanctuary school policy and refused to sign Trump administration compliance documents, despite receiving death threats and racist messages after a student flag incident went viral. The 800-student district, where Superintendent Wilmer Chavarria was himself detained by immigration officials last year, serves multilingual learners from across the globe and depends on federal funding for 6 percent of its budget. The district's public stance contrasts sharply with many school systems that have chosen to self-censor or avoid immigration-related policies amid federal investigations of diversity efforts and threats to education funding.

summaries.headline: Memphis Charter Schools Outpace District in Math Recovery
summaries.summary: Charter schools in Memphis have recovered from pandemic math learning losses faster than traditional public schools, with nearly one-quarter of charter students now scoring proficient on state tests compared to just under 22% in district schools. Charter math proficiency jumped from 2% in 2021 to 24% last year, surpassing pre-pandemic levels, while traditional schools remain below their earlier benchmarks despite climbing from 6.9% to 22%. Schools like Leadership Preparatory credit structured but flexible teaching approaches—what one leader calls "teacher autonomy with guardrails"—that adapt scripted curricula while maintaining consistent lesson frameworks and regular data review.

summaries.headline: Colorado Students Show Continued Math Gains, Mixed Literacy Results
summaries.summary: Colorado students posted higher math proficiency rates in nearly every grade on preliminary 2026 CMAS results, with fourth-grade math rising to 39 percent from 36.5 percent last year and eighth-grade climbing to 37.8 percent from 34.7 percent. Literacy results showed a mixed pattern, with fourth-grade scores jumping to 47 percent from 42 percent while eighth-grade dropped slightly to 42.2 percent from 43.9 percent. The pattern mirrors national trends of modest math recovery paired with stagnant reading performance, suggesting different subject areas may require distinct post-pandemic intervention strategies.

summaries.headline: Small Districts Get Extra Year for Web Accessibility Compliance
summaries.summary: Small K-12 districts serving 50,000 or fewer residents now have until April 26, 2028 to make their websites, learning platforms, and mobile apps conform to updated ADA Title II web accessibility standards that require captioned videos, alt text for images, and screen reader-compatible documents. The Department of Justice has adopted Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.1, Level AA as the technical standard, but most small districts face significant challenges with limited budgets, lean IT teams, and years of existing digital content that wasn't built for accessibility. The extended timeline creates breathing room for districts to systematically inventory their digital assets and train staff on creating accessible content going forward, though the scope of retrofitting existing materials remains daunting for resource-constrained schools.

summaries.headline: Florida Allocates $4.5 Billion for Vouchers Despite Audit Concerns
summaries.summary: The Florida Legislature finalized a budget that maintains $4.5 billion in voucher funding while restricting new teacher salary increases to classroom educators with at least 10 years of experience in Florida public schools. The $201 million Teacher Salary Increase Allocation caps individual raises at $3,000 and creates uneven district impacts based on workforce tenure, with Miami-Dade's 15-year average teacher experience creating different outcomes than districts with younger staff. The spending plan sidesteps new accountability measures for voucher programs despite recent auditor findings of administrative challenges, while the Florida Education Association has filed suit claiming the funding levels violate the state constitution's public education requirements.

summaries.headline: Virginia Budget Deadlock Leaves School Districts Planning Blindly
summaries.summary: Virginia school leaders face mounting uncertainty as state lawmakers remain deadlocked over a two-year budget that must pass by July 1 to ensure adequate funding for special education, at-risk students, and educator compensation. The impasse centers on whether to eliminate a $1.6 billion annual tax exemption for data centers, with the Senate supporting elimination to fund education and transportation while the House and Governor Spanberger want to preserve the break until 2035. School boards across the commonwealth must finalize staffing decisions and program budgets without knowing their state funding levels during a nationwide teacher shortage.

summaries.headline: Colorado's First 'Public Christian' School Closes After Nine Months
summaries.summary: Riverstone Academy, a 30-student school that backers called "Colorado's first public Christian school," has closed permanently after changes in state law cut off its public funding. The Pueblo County school faced multiple setbacks during its brief existence, including safety problems that forced a relocation and a $20,000 settlement with parents, while emails revealed the school was created at the behest of a conservative law firm to spark a Supreme Court case on religious liberty. The closure ends what was designed as a test case for public funding of religious education, with the school's legal challenge failing to gain the traction its backers had hoped for.

summaries.headline: Detroit Demolishes Historic High School Despite Preservation Plans
summaries.summary: Detroit Public Schools Community District will demolish the entire Cooley High School building this summer, reversing earlier plans to preserve portions of the 1928 structure for a planned $25 million sports complex. Superintendent Nikolai Vitti cited years of safety concerns, arson attacks, and blight issues, noting that preserving just the historic façade would have added $2 million to project costs. The full demolition signals how facility maintenance challenges can override historic preservation goals even when districts secure significant capital funding for redevelopment projects.

summaries.headline: Chronic Absenteeism Affects One in Five Students
summaries.summary: Students across 31 states continue to miss significant amounts of school, with one in five meeting the threshold for chronic absenteeism in the 2024-25 school year. The analysis shows improvement from pandemic peaks, as "extreme" chronic absenteeism dropped from 41% in 2021-22 to 23% in 2024-25, though rates remain well above pre-pandemic levels. District leaders face persistent attendance challenges that directly undermine learning time and academic recovery efforts four years after schools reopened.

summaries.headline: Colorado Library District Tackles Summer Learning Loss
summaries.summary: The Pikes Peak Library District launched a summer literacy program requiring participants to read or engage in activities for 30 days to earn prizes. The program serves all ages and includes additional family events like storytimes, teen programming, and summer celebrations with live music. Library-school partnerships like this offer districts a model for addressing summer slide through community resources that require minimal school staffing during break periods.

summaries.headline: Gates Foundation Opens $8 Million AI Tutoring Grant
summaries.summary: Digital Promise has released a request for proposals for an $8 million Gates Foundation grant to build open-source AI tutoring infrastructure specifically for K-12 math learning. The grant targets a single team that can address current AI limitations in tutoring, including models that give away answers too quickly, miss student motivation cues, and fail to support productive struggle through math problems. The 30-36 month project aims to create public infrastructure that districts, researchers, and developers can use rather than a commercial product, potentially reshaping how AI supports personalized math instruction across schools.

summaries.headline: Study Abroad Leaders Push Preventive Mental Health
summaries.summary: Education abroad professionals are shifting from crisis response to preventive mental health strategies as student wellness concerns increasingly disrupt international programs. SafeAbroad will present alongside university leaders at a June conference exploring how institutions can identify risks early and strengthen student resilience before problems escalate into emergencies. The focus on prevention reflects growing recognition that mental health challenges abroad require proactive risk management frameworks rather than reactive crisis intervention.

summaries.headline: Library Expands Health Programming Into Summer Reading
summaries.summary: The Lawton Public Library is integrating health literacy events into its comprehensive summer programming, offering activities like Yoga in the Park, Zumba, and Summer Solstice Yoga alongside traditional reading programs for all ages. Community engagement librarian Tanya Organ highlighted these wellness activities as part of the library's June programming, which also includes teen-focused events and cultural programming like the 2026 Lawton Chautauqua. Libraries increasingly serve as community health hubs, positioning literacy and wellness as interconnected elements of student and family support outside traditional school hours.

synthesis.topic_title: School Funding Battles Move to Courtrooms and Ballot Boxes
synthesis.whats_happening: School districts nationwide are bypassing traditional state funding channels, turning to local ballot measures and legal challenges to secure adequate resources. Districts report navigating what superintendents call 'new realities' of funding that demand longer-term strategic planning beyond annual budget cycles.
synthesis.whats_driving: State funding formulas continue failing to meet district needs, forcing local communities to shoulder greater financial responsibility through voter-approved measures. Legal pressure is mounting as districts challenge systemic underfunding through court systems, while accountability demands intensify around existing resource allocation.

- Legal challenges against state funding systems are escalating as districts seek court-ordered fixes to inequitable distribution formulas
- District leaders face pressure to demonstrate accountability and transparency in how current funding is being utilized
- Multi-year budget planning is replacing traditional annual cycles as districts adapt to funding uncertainty

local_articles.title: Jefferson Voters Pass Education Budget, Add Funds for Guidance Counselor
local_articles.summary: Jefferson Voters Pass Education Budget, Add Funds for Guidance Counselor  The Lincoln County News
local_articles.full_content:
![Jefferson residents vote for the an article pertaining to the education budget on Wednesday, May 20 at Jefferson Village School. Residents passed the $9.3 budget after adding in funds for a guidance counselor position. (Christine Simmonds photo)](https://lcnme.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/JEFeducation-CS-2col-color-800x533.jpg)

Jefferson residents vote for the an article pertaining to the education budget on Wednesday, May 20 at Jefferson Village School. Residents passed the $9.3 budget after adding in funds for a guidance counselor position. (Christine Simmonds photo)

Jefferson voters approved the education budget for the upcoming fiscal year on Wednesday, May 20 after passing an amendment to add funding for a guidance counselor position.

Those in favor of the amendment said guidance counselors provide essential services, and the cost was a small one relative to the $9,420,325.75 budget, an increase of $54,078.95 or 0.5% from last year.

Those against the amendment said the cost was too high for a job which could be performed by other staff members and expressed concern the increase would prompt a repeat of last year’s education budget vote which took six months and three elections to pass.

Jefferson School Committee member Wayne Parlin said he personally did not think the position was needed.

“We have social workers and psychiatrists on staff here, and school nurses,” he said.

Paula Schuster, a Jefferson resident and Nobleboro Central School teacher, said she was really upset this position had been cut from the budget. District psychologists and social workers often only work with students who have an individualized education program, or IEP, she said. Meanwhile there were other students experiencing trauma, suicidal tendencies and engaging in self-harm, she said.

The Jefferson School Committee cut the guidance counselor position from the budget in February when they learned the grant that paid for half the position would not be available after March 31.

When the committee learned in mid-March that funding would be available until the end of December, Danielle Bernier, the committee’s chair at the time, made motion to restore the position in the budget. It did not receive a second.

AOS 93 Business Manager Emily Komiega said the funding was from a five-year Expanding Access in School Environments grant. According to the Maine Department of Education website, these grants would invest $9 million in nine “high-need” school administrative units to increase student access to mental health professionals. The money was distributed by the Maine Department of Education and approved as part of the Bipartisan Safer Community Act.

The grant awarded AOS 93 $67,947 per year for five years, and the upcoming school year would have been number four. However, the grant funding status kept changing, Komiega said the school committee’s position was that the grant funded the job, so they would eliminate the position if they were going to keep losing the grant.

The original proposed education budget line for student and staff support, which was where funds for the guidance counselor position were couched, was recommended by the Jefferson School Committee, Jefferson Budget Committee, and the Jefferson Select Board at $374,592.70, a decrease of $6,1596.30 or 14.04% from the 2025-2026 budget.

The amendment to add $120,000 to that line item in order to fully fund a guidance counselor regardless of the Expanding Access in School Environments grant was approved by a vote of 26-16.

Elsewhere in the budget, the largest cost center increase can be seen in facilities and maintenance, which totals $852,338.20, an increase of $187,590 or 28.22%.

Komiega said the increase had two causes. The school was increasing the facilities manager from four to five days per week, and the committee reserved $100,000 in capital improvements.

Komiega said it is standard practice is to set aside money for capital improvements when there is a decrease in budget. The capital improvements fund is for unexpected expenses related to building maintenance.

The system administration budget totals $340,218.91, an increase of $55,414.48 or 19.46%. Komiega said the increase is due to the formation of the Johns Bay Coastal Alliance Education Service Center by Bristol and South Bristol. Due to the two towns leaving AOS 93, Jefferson and Nobleboro must absorb the cost of the central office.

Komiega said central office will also be reduced from 11 staff members to five.

Other instruction totals $49,767.04, an increase of $6,565.04 or 15.20%. Komiega said the increase is the cost of transporting students for sporting events.

Decreases in the budget can be seen in transportation and buses, which totals $601,191.07, a decrease of $73,309.40 or 10.87%. Komiega said this decrease comes from moving special education students back to Jefferson Village School from previous out-of-district placements.

Jefferson residents will consider validating the education budget at the polls on Tuesday, June 9. Voting will be open from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. at Jefferson Village School, at 48 Washington Road. For more information, call 549-7401 or go to [jeffersonmaine.org](http://jeffersonmaine.org/).

![](https://i0.wp.com/localnewsmatters.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/LNM-20260522-SCHOOLBONDS-01.jpg?fit=1200%2C900&ssl=1)AI ILLUSTRATION: Voters in Lafayette, Moraga and Walnut Creek are voting on a trio of parcel tax measures on the June 2 ballot aimed at supplementing local school district budgets. (AI illustration by Glenn Gehlke/Local News Matters via ChatGPT)

Two measures to benefit school districts in Contra Costa County cities were at the two-thirds vote thresholds needed to pass in early returns Tuesday night, with one other measure nearly there.

All three measures would benefit districts in the cities of Moraga, Lafayette and Walnut Creek and would go to elementary and middle schools in their districts.

Measure I in Moraga School District was passing with 68% of the vote in the first returns posted at 8 p.m.

In the Lafayette School District, Measure H appears destined to pass, with 74% of voters approving it so far.

Measure L in the Walnut Creek School District was at 62% approval in early returns, short of the two-thirds threshold.

PHOENIX — Calling it an illegal intrusion on their authority, Republican legislative leaders are moving to block or delay [a court order requiring them to fix](https://tucson.com/news/state-regional/education/article_a0e7bf75-b179-450e-a36b-85a11621476e.html) the system of funding public schools.

A judge previously ruled that system unconstitutionally leaves some students in buildings needing major repairs and without the equipment necessary to learn.

Attorneys for Senate President Warren Petersen and House Speaker Steve Montenegro are telling the state Court of Appeals that the directive by Maricopa County Superior Court Judge Dewain Fox is flawed.

They argue that the judge exceeded his authority because it is solely up to the Legislature to determine education policy. They're saying lawmakers — not the courts — set the standards that students must meet and then decide what minimum facilities are needed and, by extension, how much to spend.

But attorneys representing school districts and education groups said nothing in the court order interferes with legislative prerogative.

They pointed out it was the Legislature itself that directed what was originally known as the School Facilities Board to craft the standards. That came after a 1994 Arizona Supreme Court ruling that voided the school finance system in place at the time.

![School funding](<Base64-Image-Removed>)

House Speaker Steve Montenegro, left, and Senate President Warren Petersen look on as Gov. Katie Hobbs speaks in 2025. Montenegro and Petersen are going to court seeking to block or delay a judge's order to fix the state's school funding system.

Howard Fischer, Capitol Media Services


In turn, that led to the creation of "minimum adequacy guidelines.''

But it was shown at trial, lawyers for the schools said, that lawmakers have not provided the money for all school districts to meet the standards that they ordered created. They said that violates the constitutional requirement for the Legislature to maintain and fund a "general and uniform public school system.''

## Judge set deadline

Fox, in his 114-page decision released in August, said many schools lack the resources to ensure students have what they need to learn, including equipment and well-kept buildings.

He cited a laundry list of unmet needs, including, in some cases, buildings that are unsafe because of cracks and other deficiencies.

Also missing, the judge said, was the money to fund a requirement in the state standards for certain academic equipment, such as computers for students. Fox said the state has also failed to provide the money for other legally required improvements, including keeping students safe from shooters invading schools.

The judge did not direct how to fix all that, however.

Instead, he gave lawmakers and the governor until early November to come up with — and fund — a system that ensures schools have what they need to meet those "minimum adequacy guidelines."

Part of that is because Fox conceded he doesn't have the authority to order a specific resolution, or to direct lawmakers to allocate a specific amount of money for a problem that both sides agree could cost billions to correct.

If the November deadline is not met, the judge could bar the state from maintaining an education funding system that does not meet the requirements for adequate facilities and other capital needs. And that means if the state does not come up with a constitutionally acceptable plan, Fox could simply block the state treasurer from distributing any funds at all to any schools — something that would effectively shut down the K-12 system.

## Legislative leaders: 'Money is finite'

It is that deadline that the GOP legislative leaders want the Court of Appeals to delay, giving them time to argue that Fox's order to fix the problems should be voided.

All that starts with the costs. "Compliance with its edicts could require outlays totaling possibly in the billions,'' they said in their appellate court filings. "These funds do not materialize out of ether. They must either be extracted from the wallets of Arizona citizens and businesses or transferred away from other agencies and departments that provide vital health, safety, and social services.''

On top of that, they said it's unclear exactly how much cash it would take to comply with what Fox said is the constitutional standard and avoid a court order shutting down the school finance system.

For example, they told the appellate judges that the districts that sued said "building renewal'' — money for major renovations, repairs and certain upgrades to academic buildings — has been "underfunded'' by $3.8 billion.

Yet the entire state budget in the 2025 school year was about $16.2 billion, with nearly half of that already dedicated to K-12 education.

"At the risk of stating the obvious: money is finite,'' the lawyers for the GOP leaders told the appellate judges. "The state cannot print more currency. Every additional dollar allocated to school capital funding must be either obtained from Arizonans' bank accounts in the form of tax increases or siphoned from other components of the budget.''

## Schools: The system is broken, must be fixed

Attorneys for educators, however, said that doesn't paint an accurate picture.

They acknowledged the $3.8 billion figure of cumulative shortfalls. But they said that does not necessarily represent the cost of bringing the education system right now into compliance.

They also said there's nothing in Fox's order that requires all the money to be found in the first year.

But ultimately, their case revolves around the argument that, as Fox found, the system is broken, it affects the ability of students to learn, and it must be fixed.

For example, the judge in his ruling mentioned leaks in the roof of the Elfrida Elementary School.

"The leaks disrupt the learning environment because students stop what they are doing to position trash cans to collect the dripping water,'' Fox wrote.

And in Chino Valley, the judge said, classroom temperatures "can reach into the 90s, which impacts student learning.''

All of that, the lawyers for the schools said, is a reason for the appellate court to refuse to delay Fox's order and deadline.

"The superior court's ruling documented a massive number of problems that existed for many years and continue to exist today,'' they said.

![School funding](<Base64-Image-Removed>)

Attorneys for school boards and their clients in 2017 on the steps of a Glendale school when they filed the lawsuit seeking a declaration that the funding system for capital needs was inadequate.

Howard Fischer, Capitol Media Services


In seeking a delay, however, attorneys for the GOP leaders said they haven't flatly refused to fix problems. Instead, they said questions of the timing and prioritization of the funds that are made available are beyond the reach of the courts.

"Nonsense,'' responded the lawyers for the schools.

"Children get one shot at elementary school,'' the attorneys for schools wrote. "A child in Chino Valley who spent her education in 90-degree classrooms while the district waited more than a decade for an HVAC replacement does not benefit from a remedy that may arrive after she is done with school."

Ditto, they said, of children in schools with leaking roofs, excessive carbon dioxide buildup, mold and inadequate air conditioning. "These are Arizona children, not widgets,'' they said.

The lawyers for GOP lawmakers, in seeking to void Fox's orders, have another argument.

What's missing, they are telling the Court of Appeals, is any evidence that students are not getting an adequate education.

"Representatives of the very school districts that the trial court deemed ostensibly underfunded — including Crane, Tolleson Elementary, Blue Ridge, Wickenburg, Mohawk, Laveen, and Somerton — all testified that they provide their students with an education outcome that meets the state's minimum academic standards,'' the lawyers argued.

"They offered no examples of students at their schools whose educational experience did not meet those standards,'' they continued. "These admissions and omissions, which the trial court ignored, extinguished the plaintiffs' claims.''

But the attorneys for the schools said such a direct link between deficiencies and outcomes is not necessary for a finding of inadequate funding and an order to fix the problems.

"For example, a teacher in a sweltering, noisy, moldy classroom with excessive CO2 and a leaking roof can technically 'teach' a lesson aligned with academic standards,'' they said. "But it would be impossible to show that a certain deficiency caused specific students to fail a test.''

They said that's why state law and regulations define minimum acceptable guidelines of the quality and quantity of facilities students need to achieve high academic standards.

They also pointed out that the state's own School Facilities Board — the one created by lawmakers after they lost the 1994 ruling — itself links those guidelines directly to student performance. In fact, the expert witness called by the GOP lawmakers in the case conceded at trial that "your leaking roof I would expect to be tied to student performance, because students don't do well when the roof is leaking.''

The appellate court has not set a date to hear arguments about delaying Fox's order.

## Governor's role

Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs, for her part, has been pretty much silent on the dispute.

Her last comment came after the August ruling when she said she was aware of it but had not seen the order setting the deadline. Instead, she provided a general comment about how she has "worked diligently" with lawmakers to address underfunding in facilities.

But the judge, in that ruling, said the governor is not blameless.

He pointed out that in planning for the 2024-25 school year, the School Facilities District — the successor to the School Facilities Board which is responsible for funding construction and repairs — estimated it needed more than $587 million to meet all identified needs of all the schools. Yet the Department of Administration, which is under the governor's purview, requested less than $222 million.

There was no response to repeated requests to the governor's press aide for comments about the case, her funding plans and her own role in the problem.

# Oakland County school funding millage headed to August ballot

Published: June 3, 2026 at 5:09 PM

Oakland County voters will decide in August on a proposed 1.5 mill increase in property taxes to fund schools, which would raise taxes by $300 a year on a $200,000 home and provide an additional $781 per student annually for six years. Supporters argue the funds are necessary to address rising school costs and maintain competitiveness with neighboring counties, while opponents express concern about the growing tax burden, especially for those struggling financially or without children in the schools.

Over the last few weeks, I’ve had many people ask me about the impacts of this spring’s legislation on school districts, particularly our district. I’ve also been reminded just how complicated school funding can be, especially given the confusion and misinformation surrounding some of these changes. Three issues in particular have significant implications for Grand Rapids Area Schools (GRAS) and many other districts across the state: changes to compensatory revenue, seasonal recreational tax base replacement aid, and the proposed Permanent School Trust Fund constitutional amendment. While these topics are technical, they matter a great deal because they directly impact the financial stability of rural and regional school districts like ours.

# Cherargei calls for audit of school funding amid concerns over student congestion

Thursday 04th June, 2026 02:41 PM\|By [Emmanuel Rono](https://peopledaily.digital/author/emmanuelrono "Posts by Emmanuel Rono")

![Cherargei calls for audit of school funding amid concerns over student congestion](https://peopledaily.digital/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/653811179_1408154944685599_8859874087007292575_n-768x528.jpg)Nandi Senator Samson Cherargei during a parliamentary session on Wednesday, March 18, 2026. PHOTO/https://www.facebook.com/ParliamentKE

[Nandi Senator Samson Cherargei](https://peopledaily.digital/news/senator-cherargei-pushes-for-stronger-pwd-inclusion) has faulted the Ministry of Education for failing to conduct regular inspections in schools and for failing to account for funds allocated to learning institutions, saying proactive oversight is necessary to prevent crises in the education sector.

Speaking during an interview with a local station on Thursday, June 4, 2026, Cherargei criticised what he described as a reactive approach by education authorities, in which action is taken only after problems emerge.

“ _Ni muhimu kwa Wizara ya Elimu kuhakikisha inafanya ukaguzi wa mara kwa mara shuleni, badala ya kusubiri hadi majanga yanapotokea ndipo ianze kutangaza hatua za kuchukua,”_ Cherargei said.

![Julius Ogamba during the launch of the Teacher Wellness and Engagement Research Report. PHOTO@EduMinKenya/X](https://peopledaily.digital/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/HJQC3QGWoAAyq4_-500x343.jpg)Julius Ogamba during the launch of the Teacher Wellness and Engagement Research Report. PHOTO@EduMinKenya/X

Loosely translate: “The Ministry of Education needs to ensure it carries out regular inspections in schools instead of waiting for disasters to occur before announcing measures to address them,” Cherargei said.

According to Senator Cherargei, the Senate and the national assembly should summon Education Cabinet Secretary Julius Ogamba to explain how funds allocated to schools are being utilised.

He said a parliamentary inquiry into education financing could help establish the root causes of the persistent congestion witnessed in some schools across the country.

![Senate during a past session. PHOTO/https://www.facebook.com/ParliamentKE/FB](https://peopledaily.digital/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/senate-500x344.webp)Senate during a past session. PHOTO/https://www.facebook.com/ParliamentKE/

_“Bunge la Seneti linapaswa kumwita Waziri wa Elimu ili awasilishe maelezo kuhusu matumizi ya fedha zinazotengwa kwa ajili ya shule, hivi tutaweza kubaini chanzo cha msongamano mkubwa wa wanafunzi shuleni, hata wakati huu ambapo uchunguzi wa utumishi unaendelea,” Cherargei said._

“The Senate should invite the Education Cabinet Secretary to provide details on the use of funds allocated to schools. This will enable us to identify the source of the severe overcrowding being experienced in schools, even as investigations by relevant authorities continue,” he said.

## Utumishi investigations

This comes as the investigations into the Utumishi fire tragedy that claimed the lives of 16 girls continue.

A Naivasha Magistrates Court has detained nine Utumishi Girls’ Academy students for 21 days to allow the Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI) to complete investigations into the fire that engulfed an upper floor of one of the dormitories.

![Naivasha Law courts](https://peopledaily.digital/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/GvPTbHBXUAAIpJy-500x240.jpg)Naivasha Law Courts. PHOTO/@thetimeskenya/X

In a ruling delivered by the Chief Magistrate Abdulqadir Lorot on Wednesday, June 3, 2026, the court has noted that it has been persuaded that the respondents (nine students) ought to be detained as prayed by the DCI.

[However, Magistrate Lorot has stated that he has shortened the 30 days that had been sought and granted the investigators 21 days instead to conclude investigations to determine whether they will be charged.](https://peopledaily.digital/news/naivasha-court-detains-9-utumishi-girls-academy-students-for-21-days)

“I now allow the application; the nine respondents’ suspects will be detained at Nakuru Children Remand Home for a period of 21 days from today,” Chief Magistrate Lorot ruled.

Public university teachers have demanded a massive 300 percent increase in the higher education budget for fiscal year 2026-27, warning that financial stress across institutions is reaching a critical level. They said urgent government intervention is necessary to prevent disruption in academic operations and maintain institutional stability.

Moreover, the All Public Universities Teachers Association stated that higher education funding has remained largely stagnant since 2018. As a result, universities continue to face growing pressure, while rising inflation and operational costs have further worsened their financial situation over time.

> **Read more : [Elite Lahore schools resist free education law enforcement](https://dailytimes.com.pk/1408469/elite-lahore-schools-resist-free-education-law-enforcement/)**

The association also highlighted that many public universities are struggling to pay salaries and pensions on time. Consequently, teachers warned that the financial crisis could deepen further if immediate relief and increased funding are not provided in the upcoming budget cycle.

In addition, teachers specifically pointed out that several institutions in Islamabad, including Quaid-e-Azam University, International Islamic University, and Urdu University, are among the most affected. They demanded targeted financial support to help these universities meet essential operational and academic requirements.

> **Read more :[Punjab launches major education reforms](https://dailytimes.com.pk/1478699/punjab-launches-major-education-reforms/)**

Furthermore, the association stressed that underfunding has severely impacted both teaching quality and research output in public universities. They argued that continued neglect of the sector poses a long-term risk to students, academic development, and national intellectual growth.

Meanwhile, APUBTA urged both federal and provincial governments to coordinate efforts and address the financial crisis collectively. Teachers emphasized that without a substantial increase in funding, higher education institutions may face even greater instability in the coming months.
